questions.prompt: An instruction set architecture is best described as
options: The contract a program can rely on: instructions, registers, and their visible effects
The physical layout of the transistors
The operating system’s scheduler
A particular brand of assembler
questions.explanation: Two chips can implement one ISA with different pipelines. Programs see the contract, not the transistor floorplan.

questions.prompt: In a load/store instruction set, arithmetic operands come from
options: Registers; memory is reached only by explicit load and store
Main memory on every add, with no registers
The disk controller
The page table only
questions.explanation: Load/store machines keep the ALU on registers. Memory traffic is a separate, visible instruction.
traps: “RISC” is not only “fewer opcodes”. The memory rule is the sharper line.

questions.prompt: In ADD R1, 5 the 5 is an immediate. That means
options: The value 5 is encoded in the instruction itself
5 is a memory address that must be loaded first
5 is a device number
The assembler deletes the 5
questions.explanation: An immediate operand travels inside the instruction word. No extra memory read is required to find the 5.

questions.prompt: Which of these are real addressing ideas?
options: Register: the operand is already in a named register
Immediate: the operand bits sit in the instruction
Base plus offset: a register plus a constant forms an address
Psychic: the CPU guesses the address from the opcode color
questions.explanation: Register, immediate, and base-plus-offset are standard ways to name an operand. The last one is not.

options: The program counter, so the next fetch uses the target address
Only the destination register of the previous ADD
The disk inode
The cache block size
questions.explanation: A branch is a write to the PC, gated by a flag. If the condition is false, the PC keeps the sequential successor.

options: A readable encoding of machine instructions, translated by an assembler
The text the processor fetches from memory
A language with a garbage collector
A file system
questions.explanation: The CPU fetches numbers. An assembler turns mnemonics and labels into those numbers.
traps: The processor does not fetch the mnemonic text.

questions.prompt: What is R1 when this program halts?
questions.explanation: SUB R1, R1 writes 7 − 7 = 0. Adding R1 to itself then keeps 0. The 7 does not survive the subtract.
traps: Reading SUB R1, R1 as “subtract one” instead of “subtract the register from itself”.
questions.code:
MOV R1, 7
SUB R1, R1
ADD R1, R1
HLT

questions.prompt: A call that saves a return address on a stack typically
options: Writes the address and moves the stack pointer
Clears every register
Switches the machine from little-endian to big-endian
Deletes the caller
questions.explanation: The return address has to survive the callee. A stack push stores it and leaves a new top of stack for the callee’s locals.

questions.prompt: Give one concrete difference between a typical RISC ISA and a typical CISC ISA.
questions.answer: RISC designs favor a regular load/store set. CISC designs often allow arithmetic to name a memory operand directly.
questions.explanation: Both still need a written contract. The difference students should be able to say out loud is where an ADD is allowed to find its bits.
